author: Robert M. Pirsig
biz: Make the recognisers write the standard

Pirsig could not define quality in student writing but could grade it, so he let the people who recognised it do the defining. Try that this week at HomeownersLoan. Pull twenty recent recorded calls, have two colleagues independently mark each one as a good conversation or not, and only then write down what the good ones had in common. That becomes your call standard rather than an inherited one. Measure, against the previous month, the proportion of calls in which the adviser checked the customer's understanding of the broker fee and the secured risk, and your complaint rate.
A stuckness rule for stalled cases

Value rigidity is the expensive trap at Debt Support Direct, because an adviser who has decided the answer in the first two minutes stops hearing the client. Add a stuckness rule. Any case with no movement for fourteen days goes to a five minute review in which the adviser states the client's own stated objective out loud before anything else, with no new recommendation allowed in that meeting. Measure the number of cases stalled beyond fourteen days, and the share of clients reaching a suitable, documented outcome, split by adviser.

b: Robert Maynard Pirsig was born in Minneapolis on the sixth of September 1928, into a house where reason was the family trade. His father Maynard taught at the University of Minnesota Law School from 1934 and was its dean from 1948 to 1955. His mother was Harriet Marie Sjobeck. The boy was quick enough that an often repeated story has him tested at an intelligence quotient of a hundred and seventy at the age of nine, a figure best treated as family legend rather than measurement.

He skipped grades at the Blake School, and in May 1943, aged fourteen, he collected a high school diploma from University High School in Minneapolis, where he had edited the yearbook. Then he went to the University of Minnesota to read biochemistry.

What happened there is the seed of everything else. He was not studying science as a career. He was studying it because he believed it told the truth, and then he noticed something about the scientific method that would not let him go. When you sit down to explain a result, hypotheses do not arrive one at a time to be tested and killed off. They arrive in crowds. The better your mind, the faster they breed, and the number of experiments you can actually run in a lifetime does not increase at all.

If that is right, he reasoned, then science is not closing in on a single truth. It is producing candidate truths faster than it can eliminate them. The method he trusted was, by its own logic, running away from the answer.
He could not put it down, and his marks collapsed. The university expelled him. He was still a teenager, and he had just found the hole at the bottom of the only thing he believed in.

b: In 1946 he enlisted in the United States Army and was posted to South Korea, where he stayed until 1948. The book he wrote decades later describes that country as the place where he first glimpsed a way of seeing that does not divide the world into observers and things observed. The surviving record confirms the posting and nothing more, so take the revelation as his own telling.
Discharged, he spent several months in Seattle and then went back to the university that had thrown him out, this time to read philosophy. He took his bachelor's degree in 1950.

Then comes a stretch of life that sounds invented. He and his wife worked at the Nevada Club in Reno, saved what they could, and moved to Acayucan in Mexico with the stated intention of writing a great book. It did not get written. He studied philosophy at Banaras Hindu University in the city of Benares on the Ganges, and that is where the Eastern half of his mind was actually furnished.

The story he told about leaving is the one worth keeping. In a lecture hall, a professor explained that the destruction visited on Japan at the end of the war was, properly understood, illusory along with everything else. Pirsig asked whether a man standing underneath it would have found it illusory. He got no answer he could use, and he stopped attending. He wanted a philosophy that could not shrug at a ruined city.
He married Nancy Ann James on the tenth of May 1954. Chris was born in 1956 and Ted in 1958. That same year he took a master's degree in journalism from Minnesota, and went west to teach.

b: In 1958 he began teaching writing at what was then Montana State College in Bozeman, and stayed two years. Accounts differ over whether his title was professor or instructor, which tells you how thinly this period is documented outside his own version of it.

What he taught was composition, and composition is where his old problem came back wearing different clothes. He had to grade student writing, which meant telling students what counted as good. Trying to do it, he found that he could not define the thing he was grading while being perfectly able to recognise it. So could every student in the room.

He ran an experiment. He stopped giving grades. He told the class he would mark nothing until the end of term and would simply tell them what he thought. The weaker students were frightened, having nothing to aim at. The better ones, after a few weeks of panic, began writing in order to find out whether a sentence was any good, which is the only decent reason for writing anything.

Out of that came his word. Quality. Not a property sitting in the writing and not a reaction sitting in the reader, but the event in which the two meet, arriving before either has been sorted into place. You know it on contact. The definition comes afterwards, if it comes at all.

He also gave the university a name he meant seriously. The Church of Reason: an institution whose real business is not buildings or degrees but the honest pursuit of understanding, which means its true body might be one person thinking clearly, and everything else a very expensive shell.

b: He went to Chicago, to a programme with one of the grandest names in American higher education, the Committee on the Analysis of Ideas and Study of Methods, and there he tried to carry his idea into the heart of the discipline that owned it.

His case ran roughly like this. We are taught that the world divides into subjects and objects, mind and matter, and that quality is a soft opinion the subject adds afterwards. Pirsig turned that round. Quality comes first. It is the undivided edge of the present moment, and subjects and objects are what we cut out of it afterwards for convenience.

The cutting tool he called the analytic knife. Reason is magnificent at dividing the world into parts, every cut is a choice, and the cuts are not in the world. Classify a motorcycle by its components and you get one machine. Classify it by its functions and you get a different one. Both are true and neither is the motorcycle.

Then he went after the villain. In the Greek of Homer and the Sophists, excellence was arete, a single word covering what we now split into goodness, beauty, skill and truth. Pirsig's reading of Plato is that philosophy's founding act was to subordinate arete to Truth, making the Good a branch of knowledge, and that the whole Western habit of treating quality as decoration follows from that one demotion.

Whether he had Plato right is a serious question, and people who know the Greek better have doubted it. What is not in doubt is what the argument cost him. He was taking on two and a half thousand years with no standing in the field and very little sleep.

b: Between 1961 and 1963 he was in and out of psychiatric hospitals. The diagnosis recorded was schizophrenia. He was given electroconvulsive therapy on numerous occasions, a count nobody has published. His wife petitioned for divorce during that period. He was in his early thirties and he had been taken apart.

When he came back he was, by his own account, somebody slightly different. The book handles this by giving the earlier man a separate name, Phaedrus, after the character in Plato's dialogue, and writing about him in the third person as a ghost gaining on the narrator mile by mile across the American west. Phaedrus is brilliant, relentless and frightening, and the narrator is afraid of turning back into him.

It is worth being careful here. The split is a device chosen by a writer, not a clinical record, and the book never claims to be a case history. What the device does beautifully is dramatise something very ordinary. Most people carry an earlier self who was more certain, more extreme and more alive, and most people have quietly decided not to let him drive.

The years after the hospital were unglamorous and may have saved him. He worked as a technical writer for Northern Pump, later Northern Ordinance, and then for Honeywell in Minneapolis, writing computer manuals. For two of the four years in which he wrote his book he was producing manuals by day and the book at a kitchen table in the small hours before work.

Technical writing is the right trade for the argument he was making. A manual is worthless unless a stranger who does not care about you can follow it, and it is written by somebody required to understand the machine completely while being allowed no opinions about it whatsoever.

b: In July 1968 he put his eleven year old son Chris on the back of a nineteen sixty six Honda Super Hawk and rode west. The trip took seventeen days. Accounts of the endpoints differ slightly, from Minneapolis to San Francisco in one telling and Minnesota to northern California in another. For the first nine days they rode with his close friends John and Sylvia Sutherland on a new BMW, who turned back in Montana.

The Sutherlands are in the book because of what John would not do. He would not maintain his own motorcycle. He would not read the manual, would not carry tools, would not listen when Pirsig explained a fault, and would stand at the roadside waiting for a mechanic with an air of injured innocence.

The scene that carries the point is small enough to miss. John's handlebars kept slipping, and the repair wanted a thin shim of metal. Pirsig offered him a strip cut from an aluminium beer can, which is close to the perfect material, soft and thin and easy to work. John was offended. A beer can was not a BMW part. The handlebars went on slipping.

Pirsig's reading of that is the hinge of the whole book. John was not being stupid. He was protecting something. He experienced technology as an alien order of being that either served him or betrayed him, and he preferred the betrayal to the humiliation of understanding it. What looks like laziness is usually fear with better manners.

The other half of the pair is Pirsig himself, outside Miles City in Montana, taking the engine down to adjust the jets and the valves because the mixture had gone rich at altitude. One man loves machines and the other loves the open road. Pirsig called them classical and romantic, and insisted the division is a wound rather than a fact.

b: The most useful thing he wrote concerns something he called gumption, an old frontier word for the enthusiasm and resourcefulness you bring to a job. Gumption is the fuel. The question that matters is not how to get more of it, but how you keep losing it.

He catalogued the leaks, named them gumption traps, and split them in two. Setbacks come from outside: the bolt that shears, the part that turns out to be the wrong size, the hour spent reassembling something back to front. Hang ups come from inside, and they are far more expensive.

The worst of the hang ups is value rigidity, which means you have already settled what the answer is, so the evidence in front of you cannot reach you. He illustrated it with the South Indian monkey trap, a hollowed coconut chained to a stake with rice inside and a hole just large enough for an open hand. The monkey reaches in, takes the rice, and cannot withdraw a closed fist. Nothing holds it there except its own valuation of the rice. The trap works because the monkey will not reconsider.

The other traps are worth naming because naming them is most of the cure. Ego, which stops you taking in new facts because they would make you look foolish. Anxiety, which makes you do too much too early and botch it. Boredom, which is a signal to stop work rather than to press on. Impatience, which comes from underestimating the job, and whose only remedy is to scale your estimate of the time upwards.

Then the line that is the real reason people keep the book. Stuckness shouldn't be avoided. The moment you have run out of ideas is not a failure, it is the one state in which a genuinely new idea can arrive, because until then you are still being pushed around by the old ones. Sit in it. Look at the machine. Do not reach for a bigger hammer.

b: It took him four years. He sent the idea out with a covering letter and a couple of sample pages to a hundred and twenty one publishers. The accounts of what came back do not agree, one saying he collected a hundred and twenty one rejections and another that twenty two replied with interest, and the honest summary is that almost everybody said no.

William Morrow said yes and paid an advance of three thousand dollars, expecting to lose it. An internal note from the publisher has survived, and it is one of the great pieces of editorial judgement. This book is brilliant beyond belief, it is probably a work of genius, and will, I'll wager, attain classic stature.

It came out in 1974 as Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, an inquiry into values. The title plays on Eugen Herrigel's Zen in the Art of Archery, and Pirsig's own introduction disposes of any confusion. The book, he wrote, should in no way be associated with that great body of factual information relating to orthodox Zen Buddhist practice. It's not very factual on motorcycles, either.

It sold fifty thousand copies in three months and has sold more than five million since, which is generally reckoned to make it the best selling philosophy book ever written. George Steiner reviewed it in the New Yorker and reached for Dostoevsky, Proust and Melville, remarking that the analogies with Moby Dick are patent. Christopher Lehmann-Haupt in the New York Times admitted he was not equipped to test the philosophy and called it intellectual entertainment of the highest order. Pirsig was given a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1974.
He had produced the strangest sort of bestseller, a book about the philosophy of technology sold to millions of people on the strength of a father, a boy and a motorbike.

b: In November 1979 Chris Pirsig was stabbed to death in a mugging outside the San Francisco Zen Center. He was twenty two. The boy on the back of the motorcycle, the one the book was partly written for, did not get to be thirty.

Pirsig wrote about it in an afterword added to later editions, and it is harder to read than any of the philosophy. He had married Wendy Kimball in December 1978. A child was conceived the following year, and the reason he gave for going ahead was that the pattern of life Chris had occupied was continuing. Their daughter Nell was the result. You can find that comforting or you can find it unbearable. He meant it as metaphysics, which was the only language he had left.

He kept working. Lila, an inquiry into morals, appeared in 1991, setting out what he called the Metaphysics of Quality, a system in which value rather than matter is the basic stuff of the world. He thought it the more important of his two books. Hardly anybody read it, and academic philosophy, which had no comfortable place for an untrained outsider rebuilding its foundations, largely declined to engage at all. The frustration stayed with him.

Montana State University gave him an honorary doctorate in philosophy on the fifteenth of December 2012. He did not attend, by all accounts because he was too frail. His Honda went to the Smithsonian in December 2019. He died at home in South Berwick in Maine on the twenty fourth of April 2017, aged eighty eight.

Where he is challenged, he usually challenged himself first. He warned readers the book was not factual. His reading of Plato is contested by better Greek scholars. His Metaphysics of Quality has never found a philosopher willing to build on it. What survived is the part he thought was merely the vehicle: that care is not a mood you bring to good work but the material good work is made from, and that the real machine you are always working on is the one holding the spanner.

connects: Csikszentmihalyi measured from the inside the state Pirsig describes from the workbench, where the person and the task stop being two separate things.
Pressfield's Resistance and Pirsig's gumption traps are the same enemy catalogued twice, once as a hostile force and once as a maintenance fault.
Marcus Aurelius and Pirsig arrive at the same practical ethics, that the whole of it is attention paid to the task actually in front of you.
note: The life here follows the published record, which does not always agree with Pirsig's own book. Sources differ over whether a hundred and twenty one publishers rejected it or twenty two of them replied with interest, over whether his Montana title was professor or instructor, and over whether the ride ended in San Francisco or elsewhere in northern California. The intelligence quotient of a hundred and seventy at nine years old is a repeated claim rather than a documented test, and the Korea revelation, the Benares lecture on the atomic bombs and the Church of Reason come from his own telling. Pirsig warned in his introduction that the book is not factual about Zen and not very factual about motorcycles, and the Phaedrus persona is a literary device rather than a clinical record, so both are flagged as such in the narrative.
recall: What did Pirsig notice about the scientific method as an undergraduate, and what did it cost him?

He realised that hypotheses multiply faster than experiments can eliminate them, so the better the mind, the further the answer recedes. He became so preoccupied with the problem that his marks collapsed and the University of Minnesota expelled him.
What experiment did he run at Montana State College, and what came out of it?

He stopped giving grades for a term and told students he would simply say what he thought. Weaker students panicked, better ones began writing to find out whether a sentence was good, and the episode produced his central term, quality, as something recognised before it can be defined.
What is a gumption trap, and what are its two kinds?

A gumption trap is anything that drains the enthusiasm and resourcefulness you bring to a job. Setbacks come from outside, such as a sheared bolt or a wrong part. Hang ups come from inside, and include ego, anxiety, boredom, impatience and value rigidity.
What is the South Indian monkey trap and what does it illustrate?

A hollowed coconut is chained to a stake with rice inside and a hole just big enough for an open hand. The monkey grabs the rice and cannot pull out a closed fist. Nothing holds it except its own valuation of the rice, which is Pirsig's picture of value rigidity.
How was the book published, and how did it sell?

Pirsig approached a hundred and twenty one publishers before William Morrow accepted it with a three thousand dollar advance, expecting no profit. It appeared in 1974, sold fifty thousand copies in three months and has sold more than five million since.
recap: Robert Pirsig was born in Minneapolis in 1928 into a house of lawyers, collected his high school diploma at fourteen, and went to the University of Minnesota to read biochemistry because he believed science told the truth. There he noticed that hypotheses do not arrive one at a time to be killed off by experiment, they arrive in crowds, faster than any lifetime of experiments can dispose of them. The method he trusted was outrunning its own answers. He could not drop it, his marks collapsed, and he was expelled. He enlisted in 1946, spent two years in South Korea, came back for a philosophy degree in 1950, worked a casino floor in Reno, and studied philosophy in Benares until a lecturer told him the wartime destruction of Japan had been illusory and he walked out. In 1958 he took a master's in journalism and went to teach writing at Montana State College in Bozeman. There the old problem came back. He had to grade student writing, which meant telling students what was good, and he found he could not define it while being perfectly able to recognise it. So he stopped giving grades for a term. Out of that came his word. Quality: not a property of the thing and not a reaction in the viewer, but the undivided event in which the two meet, arriving before either has been sorted out. He took the idea to Chicago, argued that Plato's demotion of arete is where the West learned to treat value as decoration, and in 1961 he came apart. Two years in psychiatric hospitals, a diagnosis of schizophrenia, electroconvulsive therapy, a divorce petition. He came back as a technical writer, producing computer manuals by day and his book at a kitchen table before dawn. In July 1968 he rode seventeen days west with his eleven year old son Chris on a Honda Super Hawk, and built the book around two kinds of person: the friend who would not maintain his own motorcycle, and himself, adjusting valves outside Miles City. The practical heart of it is gumption, the fuel for any job, and the traps that drain it, above all value rigidity, pictured as a monkey that will not open its fist to let go of the rice. A hundred and twenty one publishers were approached, William Morrow paid three thousand dollars, and the book has sold more than five million copies. Chris was stabbed to death outside the San Francisco Zen Center in 1979, aged twenty two. Pirsig wrote about it, kept working, and died in Maine in 2017. Care is not something you bring to good work. It is what good work is made of.
stories: The beer can and the BMW

Somewhere in Montana in July 1968, John Sutherland's new BMW had handlebars that kept slipping. The repair wanted a thin shim of metal, and Pirsig had an aluminium beer can to hand, which is close to the perfect material: soft, thin and easy to cut. He offered it. John was offended. A beer can was not a BMW part, and the handlebars went on slipping for the rest of the trip. Pirsig's point was not that his friend was a fool. It was that John would rather be let down by a machine than be humbled into understanding one.
The boy who finished school at fourteen

Robert Pirsig collected his high school diploma in May 1943, aged fourteen, and went to the University of Minnesota to read biochemistry because he thought science told the truth. Then he noticed something awkward. Hypotheses do not arrive one at a time to be tested and killed, they arrive in crowds, and the quicker your mind the faster they breed, while the number of experiments you can run in a lifetime stays exactly the same. Science, by its own logic, was outrunning its own answers. He could not let it go, his marks collapsed, and the university expelled him.
One hundred and twenty one letters

Pirsig spent four years writing in the small hours before his shift as a technical writer, then sent the idea with a covering letter and two sample pages to a hundred and twenty one publishers. Almost all said no. William Morrow said yes and handed over three thousand dollars, fully expecting never to see it again. Somebody there wrote an internal note that survives: this book is brilliant beyond belief, it is probably a work of genius, and will, I'll wager, attain classic stature. It sold fifty thousand copies in three months.
take: Quality is recognised before it is defined
Stop waiting for a watertight definition of good before you demand it. Gather the people who can recognise it, mark real examples, and write the definition out of what they agreed on.
When you run out of ideas, resist the urge to do something just to be doing it. Sit with the problem and look at it. New ideas only arrive once the old ones have stopped shouting.
If the facts are not landing, suspect that you decided the answer before you looked. Say your conclusion out loud, then argue the opposite for five minutes before touching anything.
Scale the time up, not the effort
Impatience comes from underestimating the job. Double your estimate before you start, and the same work stops feeling like failure.
Pirsig treated boredom as the moment errors begin. When it arrives, break off, walk away and come back, rather than pushing through and paying for it later.
Resistance to learning a machine is usually fear
The colleague who will not touch the system is protecting themselves from looking foolish, not avoiding effort. Teach the smallest possible first step and let the fear go down on its own.
Separate the setback from the hang up
Name whether the delay came from outside or from your own state of mind. The two need completely different responses, and most people treat every problem as the first kind.
The real job is the person doing it
Treat your own attention, rest and temper as part of the equipment. A tired, defensive operator will produce poor work with perfect tools.
title: The Man Who Rode West With His Own Ghost
wiifm: You already know that caring about your work matters. What you probably do not have is a mechanic's account of why caring is a method rather than a mood, and of exactly what is happening in the hour when you lose it. Pirsig wrote the best description anybody has managed of the leaks: the ego that cannot take in new facts, the certainty that makes evidence invisible, the boredom you ought to obey. You will come away with a word for the thing you can recognise and cannot define, a named set of traps, and the oddly freeing instruction to stay stuck.
words: The Greek word for excellence, meaning a thing or a person performing its proper function superbly.
Pirsig argued that arete once covered goodness, beauty, skill and truth together, and that Plato's demotion of it is where quality became a mere opinion.
A travelling popular lecture or tent show, once common in rural America, meant to educate and entertain at the same time.
Pirsig called his roadside philosophical talks chautauquas, because they were composed to be spoken aloud to a captive passenger rather than read.
To treat an abstraction as though it were a solid thing in the world.
The book's central complaint is that we have reified the split between subject and object, mistaking a convenient cut for a feature of reality.
Travelling from place to place rather than settling, and by extension teaching while on the move, after Aristotle's walking school.
The whole book is peripatetic philosophy, worked out at fifty miles an hour between Minneapolis and the Pacific.
An obsession with a single idea that crowds out everything else.
Phaedrus's pursuit of quality tips into monomania, which is why George Steiner's review reached for Moby Dick.
